sentences.text: Caririsuchus possessed a high triangular skull featuring large, circular eyesockets that were directed more laterally.

The upper jaw likely held between 21 and 22 teeth, with four located in the premaxilla and the rest in the maxilla. All teeth possessed finely serrated edges, where front teeth were pointed and rear teeth were smaller, blunter, and more compressed. These teeth were closely spaced and arranged in an overbite rather than interlocking, similar to modern alligators.

Eric Buffetaut described Caririsuchus as one of the most heavily armored crocodilians known. Its armor extended from just behind the head to the tail tip, featuring a single double row running along the neck and torso. Individual osteoderms were rectangular, wider than long, and increased in size from the head to the mid-body before shrinking toward the hips. The midline osteoderms overlapped but lacked the articulation processes found at the anterolateral corners of some other crocodylomorphs. These osteoderms featured low, wide midline keels and ornamentation of pits radiating outward from the center of each scute.
Based on the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — Caririsuchus was a small animal measuring 1.5 meters from snout to tail tip.
It is considered one of the most heavily armored crocodilians known, with protection extending from just behind the head all the way to the tail tip.
Alexander Kellner noted that the femur was 25% larger than its humerus, suggesting a specific adaptation for movement.

Brazilian paleontologist Alexander Kellner described the new genus and species Caririsuchus camposi in 1987. The genus name honors the Kiriri people who historically inhabited the Araripe Basin in Brazil, while the species name was chosen to honor Brazilian paleontologist and geologist Diogenes de Almeida Campos.

The more complete fossil slab from which the type material was taken was illegally shipped to Europe and is now believed to be in a private collection with unknown current whereabouts. Some of the Caririsuchus remains that remained in Brazil were destroyed in a 2018 fire at the Rio de Janeiro fossil collection.
Caririsuchus fossils are found only in the Romualdo Formation in Brazil's Araripe Basin. Only one fossil occurrence of Caririsuchus has been recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
Caririsuchus was a semi-aquatic animal that lived in the coastal environment of the Romualdo Formation. It is interpreted as a semi-aquatic animal based on its broad snout.
The habitat of Caririsuchus likely included lagoons, deltas, and possibly an inland sea. Caririsuchus lived in a tropical climate that was warm and ranged from semiarid to arid.
Fossils of Caririsuchus are well preserved because the ancient seafloor had low oxygen levels.

Caririsuchus is classified as a member of the clade Notosuchia, typically placed in the clade Itasuchidae alongside relatives like Pepesuchus and Itasuchus. Eric Buffetaut was the first to classify Caririsuchus in the family Trematochampsidae, treating it as a species of Itasuchus. In 2018, Geroto and Bertini established the subfamily Pepesuchinae within Peirosauridae, including Caririsuchus as a distinct genus alongside Itasuchus, Pepesuchus, and Barreirosuchus. Caririsuchus belongs to the subfamily Pepesuchinae and is classified within the family Peirosauridae. The validity of the family Trematochampsidae is debated, with its type genus considered dubious and its members now distributed among various groups within Notosuchia. A polytomy among Caririsuchus, Itasuchus, Pepesuchus, and Roxochampsa has led to debate over whether all four should be merged into the genus Itasuchus. Some authors debate the classification of Caririsuchus, placing it in the peirosaurid subfamily Pepesuchinae instead of Itasuchidae.

Caririsuchus lived during the Early Cretaceous period. It inhabited the Romualdo Formation in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil during the Aptian to Albian stages. Caririsuchus lived during the Aptian stage, between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago.
